found: Measured: after the reboot the agent replayed the afternoon's jobs from the oldest (102 started, 40 ok, 62 failed - mostly guards refusing), fifty at a time after a reconnect, on shared clones; it had inferred 'pending' from a missing result. Before that it stalled at 22:29 CET with nothing logged until the reboot. No alert could reach the author - every channel went through the agent. Harm: none - four replayed pull requests, all the legitimate tad 0.4.0 pin bump; no direct pushes, tags, releases or phone actions; tools and clones restored. The root: a job is a script with no record of its life. Proven answers: durable execution's event history and heartbeats (Temporal), leases with fencing tokens (Kleppmann; Patterns of Distributed Systems), a dead man's switch watched from elsewhere (Healthchecks), crash-only recovery (Candea and Fox), run-once jobs with deadlines (Kubernetes), idempotency keys (Stripe), a working tree per job (git worktree). Replayed 2026-11-12: the old agent's real log of 2026-11-11, read line by line through oco-agent's rules (oco-agent/replay): of the 357 jobs the old agent started over six runs, oco-agent would have started 255 and refused exactly 102, each because it had already finished - the first at 23:16:24, the moment the replay began. The journal it kept (764 rows of tad data) checks out and answers SQL. 2026-11-12, from the whole system's log: the machine did not sleep and its network stayed up through the stall; a USB device was disconnected at 22:25:28 with nothing after it going wrong, so the phone looks innocent. The stall was inside lab-agent's daemon. Its GitHub client is built with no limit on how long a request may take (src/github.rs: ureq::AgentBuilder::new().build()), so one connection that hangs holds the polling loop for ever - which fits every fact, though nobody watched it hang. oco-agent's client limits every request to 20 s. The desktop is set to suspend after an hour without input, and lab-agent keeps it awake only while a job runs.
question: What let the 2026-11-11 incident happen, and how do proven systems prevent each part of it?

found: Waiting is one of the seven wastes of the Toyota Production System; Kanban measures flow efficiency - time worked over total time - so manual work (effort) and waiting (idle time) are two halves of one measure. Little's law: shorter waits or more work in flight raise throughput. Make and CI run independent jobs side by side and serialise only those sharing a resource. So: lab-agent records every wait itself, with what is waited on and for which project; and jobs declare the resources they hold, so those that do not conflict run in parallel.

found: tad today: a 127-line runner (check, canonical form, SQL statements on DuckDB) and a 478-line renderer of Markdown documents, vendored into four repositories (the phone project, the canon, the playbook, Rhizoid). Their schemas hold 41 tables, and every constraint is an id pattern, a list of allowed values, a required field, or one list-of-words column - no foreign keys, no SQL logic. So tables can be declared as data (Frictionless Table Schema, CSV on the Web), checked without a database engine; SQL stays a possible view onto the data (as Datasette is), not its source of truth. Dolt keeps a database in a separate store; tad keeps text in plain git, which is its point. Measured 2026-11-11: Python's check only compares field names with columns; the real validation is canon (DuckDB enforces types and rules on import), and checks/*.sql holds 13 cross-table invariants of four kinds - ids unique across tables, references resolving, everything cited, no mirrored relations - all declarable as data. Measured 2026-11-11: three of the four repositories carry an older vendored copy of the renderer (185 and 194 lines against today's 478) - copies drift silently. On the switch the canon and Rhizoid get today's renderer for the first time; their documents change (rule lines between log entries, reStructuredText if asked).
question: What must tad in Rust be, and how should it declare its tables?
